food = (
    pl.read_csv(ub + "data/wweia_food.csv", ignore_errors=True)
    .select(

### Questions

This is What We Eat in America, the dietary part of a national health survey. Each
person was asked to recall everything they ate on the previous day. A row is one food
item eaten by one person: 173,174 items reported by 11,925 people.

`id` is the person, `day_of_week` is an integer from 1 to 7, and `time` is the hour the
item was eaten. `meal_name` is what the person called the meal, `food_source` is where
the food came from, and `at_home` says whether it was eaten at home. `grams` is the mass
of the item and `kcal` is its calories.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it
to a variable.

1. Start with a warm-up. Filter to the items with more than 2,000 calories and sort
them from the most calories to the fewest.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.kcal > 2000)
    .sort(c.kcal, descending=True)
)
```

2. Count the number of items for each `meal_name` and sort from the most items to the
fewest.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.meal_name)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

Dinner, lunch, breakfast, and snack are the four big categories. Further down are
Spanish names such as `Cena` and `Almuerzo`, because some interviews were in Spanish.

3. Now let plotnine do the counting. Draw a bar plot of `meal_name` using `geom_bar`,
and add `coord_flip` so the labels are readable.

```{python}
(
    food
    .ggplot(aes(c.meal_name))
    .geom_bar()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

4. The bars in the previous plot are in no useful order. Take the code from the previous
question and sort the rows by `pl.len().over(c.meal_name)` before plotting.

```{python}
(
    food
    .sort(pl.len().over(c.meal_name))
    .ggplot(aes(c.meal_name))
    .geom_bar()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

`pl.len().over(c.meal_name)` writes the size of each meal onto every row of that meal,
so sorting on it puts the bars in order of their counts.

5. Draw the same plot a second way. Use your code from question 2 to compute the
counts, sort them from smallest to largest, and draw them with `geom_col`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.meal_name)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n)
    .ggplot(aes(c.meal_name, c.n))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

The picture is the same. `geom_bar` counts the rows for you; `geom_col` draws a number
you have already computed.

6. Some numbers are not counts, so `geom_bar` cannot draw them. Remove the rows where
`food_source` is the text `"NA"`, then compute the number of items and the mean
calories for each `food_source`. Keep the sources with at least 500 items, sort by the
mean, and draw the means with `geom_col` and `coord_flip`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.food_source != "NA")
    .group_by(c.food_source)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        mean_kcal = c.kcal.mean()
    )
    .filter(c.n >= 500)
    .sort(c.mean_kcal)
    .ggplot(aes(c.food_source, c.mean_kcal))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

An item from a fast food or pizza restaurant averages 210 calories. An item from a
grocery store averages 133.

7. Draw a histogram of `kcal` with `geom_histogram`, using `binwidth=25`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_histogram(binwidth=25)
)
```

The plot is almost a single bar. A few items have thousands of calories, which
stretches the x-axis, and 23,132 items have exactly zero calories, most of them glasses
of water.

8. Take the code from the previous question and filter to the items with more than 0
and at most 600 calories before plotting.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.kcal > 0, c.kcal <= 600)
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_histogram(binwidth=25)
)
```

The height of each bar is the number of items whose calories fall in that 25-calorie
range. Most items are small, and the counts fall off steadily after the first few bins.

9. Draw the same histogram again, but set `bins=10` instead of `binwidth`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.kcal > 0, c.kcal <= 600)
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_histogram(bins=10)
)
```

`binwidth` sets the width of each bar; `bins` sets how many bars there are. Ten bins
hides most of the shape.

10. Draw a density plot of the same filtered data with `geom_density`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.kcal > 0, c.kcal <= 600)
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_density()
)
```

11. Take the code from the previous question and set `adjust=3` inside `geom_density`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.kcal > 0, c.kcal <= 600)
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_density(adjust=3)
)
```

A larger `adjust` makes the curve smoother. A smaller one makes it follow the data more
closely.

12. Items are rarely what we care about. Group by `id` to add up each person's calories
for the day, and draw a density plot of the totals.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(kcal = c.kcal.sum())
    .ggplot(aes(c.kcal))
    .geom_density()
)
```

The curve peaks at around 1,600 calories and has a long tail to the right. Keep in mind
that this is what people *remembered* eating, which is usually less than what they ate.

13. Now compare meals. Filter to the four main meals with
`c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"])`, add up each person's
calories at each meal by grouping by `id` and `meal_name`, and draw a boxplot of the
calories for each meal with `coord_flip`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(kcal = c.kcal.sum())
    .ggplot(aes(c.meal_name, c.kcal))
    .geom_boxplot()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

14. Take the code from the previous question and order the boxes by their medians, by
sorting on `c.kcal.median().over(c.meal_name)` before plotting.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(kcal = c.kcal.sum())
    .sort(c.kcal.median().over(c.meal_name))
    .ggplot(aes(c.meal_name, c.kcal))
    .geom_boxplot()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

15. Compute by hand the three numbers that make up each box. Take the same per-person,
per-meal totals and group by `meal_name`, computing `q1` with `c.kcal.quantile(0.25)`,
`median` with `c.kcal.median()`, and `q3` with `c.kcal.quantile(0.75)`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .filter(c.meal_name.is_in(["Breakfast", "Lunch", "Dinner", "Snack"]))
    .group_by(c.id, c.meal_name)
    .agg(kcal = c.kcal.sum())
    .group_by(c.meal_name)
    .agg(
        q1 = c.kcal.quantile(0.25),
        median = c.kcal.median(),
        q3 = c.kcal.quantile(0.75)
    )
    .sort(c.median)
)
```

The medians run from 347 calories at breakfast to 639 at dinner. The middle line of each
box is the median, and the ends of the box are `q1` and `q3`.

16. Last one. Add up each person's `grams` and `kcal` for the day, then draw a scatter
plot of calories against grams with `alpha=0.05`, and add a straight line of best fit
with `geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)`.

```{python}
(
    food
    .group_by(c.id)
    .agg(
        grams = c.grams.sum(),
        kcal = c.kcal.sum()
    )
    .ggplot(aes(c.grams, c.kcal))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.05)
    .geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)
)
```

People who eat more food by weight report more calories, but the points spread widely
around the line. A lot of the weight people report is water and other drinks with no
calories.
